topic: Whether ancient philosophers had a concept of 'free will'
stance: The 'problem of determinism and free will' as conceived in contemporary philosophy was not considered by Aristotle, Epicurus, or the Stoics; it emerged in the 2nd c. CE via the conflation of Stoic and Aristotelian theories. Epicurus' swerve does not deliver 'two-sided freedom'.

topic: Origin of the notion of free will
stance: The notion of free will originates with the Stoic Epictetus (55-135 CE) — Aristotle had no notion of free will; the concept then was absorbed into late Platonism and transmitted to Origen and Augustine. Augustine derived most of his thinking on the will from Epictetan Stoicism, not original Christian discovery.

topic: Emergence of will as distinct faculty
stance: Greek philosophy long resisted formulating a distinct theory of will, grounding human action instead in knowledge and reason. The notion of an autonomous will distinct from reason and desire emerges principally with Augustine and the Christian tradition rather than in classical Greek thought.

Aristotle separates necessity from causation: actions open to moral scrutiny may be caused without being necessitated. Aristotle was an indeterminist about chance, but did not have a doctrine of libertarian human agency. Causes are primarily explanatory rather than necessitating.

topic: Discovery of the will from Aristotle to Augustine
stance: Classical Greek philosophy contains no distinct term/concept for 'will' as an independent psychological faculty; the Latin voluntas/libera voluntas emerges via Cicero, Lucretius, Seneca. Epictetus is the major authority in the discovery of the will, possibly influenced by Seneca.

Epicurus is the first ancient thinker to recognize explicitly the 'Free Will Question'; the swerve is his solution to incompatibilist worries about atomic determinism. (Position supports Huby 1967 against Bobzien.)

Chrysippus developed early compatibilist arguments reconciling causal determinism with moral responsibility, especially via the distinction between perfect/principal and proximate/auxiliary causes, and via the cylinder analogy; Alexander of Aphrodisias' De Fato is the principal hostile witness.

topic: Stoic compatibilism + ancient anticipation of contemporary debates
stance: Chrysippus advanced a 'Frankfurt-style' argument against the claim that responsibility requires the capacity to do otherwise. Three distinct compatibilist theories can be reconstructed from Chrysippus; even though events are necessitated, we are responsible when they occur through us in accordance with our nature.

topic: Stoic theory of action and psychology
stance: Reconstructs the older Stoic theory of the psychology of action — impulse (hormē), assent (synkatathesis), and impression (phantasia) — as a coherent intellectualist theory distinct from Aristotelian, Epicurean, and Platonic accounts. Stoic action arises from rational assent, not a separate faculty of will.
Stoics regarded emotions as beliefs leading to action rather than as feelings; responsibility under necessity is preserved because actions still flow from the agent's rational assent to impressions.

The atomic swerve plays no direct role in voluntary action — its effect in the soul's atomic pattern is no more than a slight declination breaking rigid determination; voluntary action is not produced by individual swerves but is preserved by the swerve's role in breaking causal necessity.

topic: Stoic theory of self and agency
stance: Hellenistic theories of self and ethical development are best read as naturalistic and 'structured' (not 'subjective' in the modern post-Cartesian sense). Stoic agency is grounded in the rational coherence of the self with cosmic nature, not in faculties of will.

The Stoics develop a sophisticated causal theory that grounds moral responsibility in agent-internal causes (cohesive cause, perfect cause) rather than necessitating external chains; the theory anticipates but does not collapse into modern compatibilism.

Origen set out to construct a Christian philosophy with the explicit intention of preserving theology from pagan-Platonist infiltration; his hermeneutics, eschatology, cosmology, and Trinitarian theology rest on an anthropology radically opposed to Platonism. Common vocabulary or parallels do not warrant the standard 'Origen-as-Platonist' reading.

Augustine adapted a deeply Platonic outlook to Christianity, constructing a vision in which Platonism and Christianity point in the same direction; his doctrine of will, love, and right action grafts Platonist eros onto Christian grace.

Celsus' attack on Christianity and Justin's apologetic response must be read in the framework of Middle Platonism; Justin's doctrine of the Logos and of human autonomy is shaped by his middle-Platonist formation (canonical reading since 1955).

topic: Early Christian philosophical engagement with Greek thought
stance: Early Christian thinkers of 2nd-4th centuries (Justin, Origen, Cappadocians) engage substantively with ancient philosophical debates on cosmogony, free will (autexousion / prohairesis), concept formation, and body-soul relation; they should be read as philosophers, not merely as theologians.

topic: Ancient philosophy as way of life
stance: Ancient philosophy is fundamentally a bios — a set of spiritual practices (askesis, dialogue, contemplation) aimed at formation of the philosophical student, not merely informing. Epictetus' three disciplines (action, assent, desire) are the 'key' to Stoic philosophy as a lived practice.

Libertarian incompatibilism — that the existence of alternative possibilities is necessary for free agency, and determinism is incompatible with it — can be defended without appeal to obscure or mysterious agency, via the notion of self-forming actions (SFAs).

The Consequence Argument: if determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the laws of nature and remote past events; since neither is up to us, our acts are not up to us. Incompatibilism + free-will-exists entails libertarianism.

Basic Argument: to be truly responsible for what one does, one must be responsible for the way one is; but ultimate self-creation (causa sui) is impossible, so no one is ultimately morally responsible for anything. Both compatibilist and libertarian accounts fail.

Moral responsibility does not require the ability to do otherwise. 'Frankfurt cases' (counterfactual interveners) show that an agent may be morally responsible even when she could not have done otherwise. This decouples moral responsibility from libertarian free will.

description: Bobzien's review of Frede 2011 ('A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought') argues against Frede's thesis that a notion of free will is genuinely present in Epictetus and the Stoics in the form Frede claims. Bobzien holds the modern 'free will' problem only emerges in the 2nd c. CE via the conflation of Stoic and Aristotelian theories.

Bobzien (2000, OSAP 19) explicitly contests the position of Huby (1967), Long, and Sedley that Epicurus discovered the free-will problem. She argues Epicurus' swerve does not deliver 'two-sided freedom' in the sense required.
Same as critique of Long: Bobzien rejects Sedley's reading that Epicurus' swerve solves a recognizably libertarian free-will problem.

Long and Sedley co-authored 'The Hellenistic Philosophers' (1987) and share the reading that Epicurus was the first ancient thinker to recognize explicitly a free-will problem; the swerve is his (controversial) response.

Kahn (1988) and Frede (2011) both argue that the concept of will as a distinct faculty is absent in classical Greek philosophy and emerges only in the Stoic-Roman period (Seneca, Epictetus) before being absorbed by Augustine. Compatible historical theses.
Dihle (1982) and Kahn (1988) converge on the view that Greek philosophy lacked a distinct faculty of will; both place its emergence in the Stoic-Roman / Christian transition.

Salles (2005) explicitly argues that Chrysippus advanced a 'Frankfurt-style' argument against the principle of alternate possibilities — an ancient anticipation of Frankfurt's 1969 thesis. Bridges ancient Stoic compatibilism to contemporary debates.
Salles' 2005 reconstruction of three Chrysippean compatibilisms positions itself in dialogue with Bobzien 1998, both reading and refining her account of perfect/auxiliary causes.
Sharples' edition/commentary on Alexander De Fato (1983) is the foundational scholarly work on which Bobzien 1998 builds; Bobzien refines and reinterprets several of Sharples' readings.

Strawson's Basic Argument (1986) targets libertarian theories like Kane's: ultimate moral responsibility is impossible because causa sui is impossible. Kane defends libertarianism against precisely this kind of skeptical move.

Frankfurt 1969 (rejection of the Principle of Alternate Possibilities) directly undercuts the libertarian incompatibilism that van Inwagen 1983 defends, since the latter assumes that responsibility requires alternative possibilities.

Edwards' 'Origen Against Plato' (2002) is methodologically positioned against the dominant 'Christian-Platonist synthesis' approach exemplified by Rist's 'Augustine: Ancient Thought Baptized' (1994). Edwards argues that scholars (like Rist for Augustine) have leapt to unjustified Platonist readings on the basis of mere shared vocabulary.
Karamanolis (2013) builds on Andresen's canonical 1955 reading of Justin Martyr in the Middle Platonist context, extending the same approach to the whole early-Christian philosophical tradition.
A.A. Long edited Frede's 1997 Sather Lectures for posthumous publication after Frede's 2007 death, restructuring the original six lectures into ten chapters.

Gill (2006) and Inwood (1985) are the two canonical reconstructions of Stoic moral psychology and the structure of agency; they share an intellectualist (anti-will-faculty) reading but disagree on the role of personality structure vs. action-theoretic primitives.
Brennan (2005) extends and partially revises Inwood (1985) on Stoic theory of action, especially regarding the role of belief vs. impulse in emotions.
Furley's 1967 reading of the swerve as causally indirect (no individual swerve produces a specific voluntary action) anticipates and conflicts with the more direct libertarian reading of Long/Sedley.
